units.t: Meal Planning Without the Misery.
Part one. The six o'clock problem.
It's six o'clock on a weeknight.
You open the fridge and stare into it, as if dinner might appear if you wait long enough.
There's half a capsicum, some yoghurt, a bag of spinach that's gone a bit slimy, and a lot of condiments.
So it's toast again, or a drive to get takeaway.
If that scene sounds familiar, this lesson is for you.
We'll build a simple weekly meal plan that takes about fifteen minutes and doesn't require you to become a different person.
First, why bother?
The most obvious reason is money.
End Food Waste Australia, a national research centre, estimates that food wasted at home costs households up to $2,500 a year.
That's about $50 a week, much of it in fresh food bought with good intentions and then forgotten at the back of the fridge.
A plan means you buy food for meals that will actually happen.
There's a health angle too.
In 2017, a team of French researchers led by Pauline Ducrot looked at the eating habits of more than forty thousand adults.
They found that people who planned their meals, even just occasionally, tended to eat a more varied diet and stick more closely to nutrition guidelines.
Planners were also less likely to be obese.
Now, that study could only show a link, not cause and effect.
As the researchers themselves pointed out, people who already care about healthy eating may simply be more likely to plan.
But it fits with what most of us know from experience.
The worst food decisions tend to happen when we're tired, hungry and out of ideas.
And that's the real point.
Deciding what to eat at six o'clock, when you're tired and hungry, is the hardest possible time to decide.
Meal planning simply moves that decision to a calmer moment.
You make it once, on a quiet morning, instead of seven times on seven tired evenings.
It saves time as well.
Without a plan, many of us duck into the shops three or four times a week for one missing thing.
And that quick trip for milk rarely ends with just milk.
One proper shop, with a list, cuts out most of those extra trips and the impulse buys that come with them.
Part two. A fifteen minute system.
Here's a simple system in four steps.
If you're driving, just listen along, and try it out on the weekend.
Step one is to pick a planning moment.
Choose a regular time each week, ideally the day before you do your main shop.
Sunday morning over a coffee works for lots of people.
Having a fixed time matters more than having a perfect plan.
Step two is to shop your own kitchen first.
Before you write anything down, look in the fridge, the freezer and the pantry.
What needs using up in the next few days?
That half a capsicum and the spinach become the start of a stir fry or a frittata, rather than going in the bin.
Planning around what you already have is where most of the savings come from.
Step three is to plan fewer meals than there are nights.
This is the part most people get wrong.
If you plan seven brand new dinners, life gets in the way.
Someone works late, a friend invites you out, or you're just too tired, and the ingredients go off.
Instead, plan four or five dinners.
Leave one night for leftovers, and one flexible night for eggs on toast, a freezer meal, or the odd takeaway without guilt.
A plan with breathing room is a plan you'll actually keep.
It also helps to give nights a loose theme.
For example, Monday could be pasta, Tuesday a stir fry, Wednesday soup, and Thursday tacos or wraps.
You're not locked into the same meal every week.
You're just choosing from a smaller set of options, which makes planning much faster.
Keep a running list of ten or fifteen meals your household actually likes, on your phone or on the fridge, and pick from that.
Step four is to write the shopping list from the plan.
Go meal by meal and write down only what's missing.
Group the list by where things are in the shop, fruit and veg together, dairy together, and so on.
You'll be quicker in the supermarket, and you'll wander past fewer tempting extras.
If you want to save a bit more, glance at the weekly specials before you plan, not after.
If chicken thighs or broccoli are on special, build a meal or two around them.
That's much cheaper than choosing meals first and then paying full price for whatever they need.
Seasonal fruit and vegetables are usually cheaper and tastier too, and frozen vegetables are a perfectly good, cheap backup that won't go off by Thursday.
What about breakfast and lunch?
Most people don't need to plan those in detail.
Pick two or three breakfasts you rotate, and make sure the ingredients are always on the list.
For lunches, leftovers do a lot of the work, and a couple of easy standbys cover the rest.
Part three. Making it stick.
A few tricks make the system much easier to live with.
The first is to cook once and eat twice.
When you make a bolognese, a curry or a soup, make a double batch.
Have one meal tonight and freeze the rest, or turn it into lunch the next day.
Over time you build up a small stock of freezer meals, which is exactly what rescues you on the flexible night.
The second is to plan ingredients that do double duty.
If you buy a bunch of coriander for tacos on Monday, put something on the plan later in the week that also uses coriander.
A roast chicken on Sunday can become wraps on Monday and soup on Tuesday.
That way, nothing is bought for one meal and left to wilt.
The third is to understand the dates on packets, because they cause a lot of needless waste.
In Australia, a use-by date is about safety.
Food shouldn't be eaten after its use-by date, even if it looks and smells fine.
A best-before date is about quality.
Food can still be safe to eat after its best-before date, as long as it isn't damaged or spoiled, though it may have lost a little freshness.
Plenty of perfectly good food gets thrown out because people treat the two as the same thing.
The fourth is to put leftovers in the fridge promptly once they've stopped steaming, and eat them within a couple of days, or freeze them.
Label them with the date, even just a scribble on masking tape.
Mystery containers are the ones that end up in the bin.
Your freezer is a great friend here too.
Bread, grated cheese, cooked rice and ripe bananas all freeze well, so anything you won't get to in time can go in there instead of the bin.
The fifth is to share the load.
If you live with other people, ask everyone to name one meal they'd like that week.
People complain less about dinners they helped choose, and older kids can take a turn cooking their pick.
The sixth is to keep an emergency pantry.
These are a handful of long-lasting basics that can always become a meal.
Think pasta, a tin of tomatoes, tinned tuna or beans, rice, eggs and some frozen peas.
With those on hand, even the night when everything goes wrong still ends in a proper dinner, in about fifteen minutes.
Replace each item as soon as you use it, so the safety net is always there.
Finally, don't aim for perfection.
Some weeks the plan will fall apart, and that's fine.
Even a rough plan for three nights beats no plan at all.
The goal is simply fewer panicked evenings, less food in the bin, and a bit more money left over.
So here are the key takeaways.
Plan once a week, starting with what's already in your kitchen, and plan fewer meals than there are nights.
Cook in batches, choose ingredients that work in more than one meal, and remember that use-by means safety while best-before means quality.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. According to End Food Waste Australia, food wasted at home can cost a household up to how much a year?
Answer. About $2,500, or roughly $50 a week.
Question two. Why should you plan fewer dinners than there are nights in the week?
Answer. To leave room for leftovers and a flexible night, so food doesn't go to waste when plans change.
Question three. What's the difference between a use-by date and a best-before date?
Answer. Use-by is about safety. Best-before is about quality.
That's the end of Meal Planning Without the Misery. Enjoy your dinner.
